content_of_post_to_comment: I age, my students do not. With each passing year, I get older. When I started teaching, I was 23 and my students were between 14 and 17. Thirty years later, here I am at 53 and my students are still the same age. In 3 years, I will be 56 and they will remain at 14, 15... in 10, I will be 63 and they will be at their eternal 14, 15... That is why I need to constantly revisit adolescence and drink from the fountains of their youth. My students will never stop being adolescents. The one who lost something in this story was me. Time does not pass for them. They are always at the peak of their adolescence. Mine is what was left behind... It is not them who need to run ahead of my extra years, it is I who must dive into their fewer years. Outside of school, they will age. And so that they age prepared for the challenges of aging, here at school I have to rejuvenate. When you realize this, your teaching practice changes completely (and for the better). Kisses & Hugs
comment: The fascinating tension is that teachers borrow youth from students, but must also teach them to outgrow the very world that keeps the teacher young. How do we preserve curiosity without delaying maturity?
